headline: FIFA scraps private investment plan for World Cup after global backlash
summary: President Gianni Infantino cancelled the proposal to allow private investors a stake in the tournament after threats of a boycott from UEFA and other football bodies.
details: FIFA President Gianni Infantino has scrapped a plan to allow private investment in the World Cup following fierce backlash from football officials worldwide.
The proposal involved creating a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), valued at $20 billion, to raise up to $4.2 billion from private investors.
If approved, the project would have provided 211 member associations with a one-off payment of $20 million each in 2027 and increased future funding allocations.
However, the move was condemned by UEFA, the AFC, and CONCACAF, with UEFA stating that the World Cup is not for sale and threatening that national teams would boycott competitions.
Pressure mounted further when senior advisor Carlos Cordeiro resigned, calling the plan a 'bad deal for football' and the long-term future of the game.
The European Union praised UEFA for defending the game's integrity, and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham described Infantino as 'the wrong man' to lead FIFA.
Infantino stated that the project was intended to strengthen member associations but was cancelled because it created divisions that were no longer in the interest of the game.
He now intends to focus on restoring harmony and continuing to grow football globally, particularly in countries that need the most support.
caption:
The World Cup is not for sale. FIFA has cancelled a $4.2 billion private investment plan after football bodies threatened a boycott.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino has scrapped a plan to allow private investment in the World Cup following fierce backlash from football officials worldwide.

The proposal involved creating a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), valued at $20 billion, to raise up to $4.2 billion from private investors.

If approved, the project would have provided 211 member associations with a one-off payment of $20 million each in 2027 and increased future funding allocations.

However, the move was condemned by UEFA, the AFC, and CONCACAF, with UEFA stating that the World Cup is not for sale and threatening that national teams would boycott competitions.

Pressure mounted further when senior advisor Carlos Cordeiro resigned, calling the plan a 'bad deal for football' and the long-term future of the game.

The European Union praised UEFA for defending the game's integrity, and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham described Infantino as 'the wrong man' to lead FIFA.

Infantino stated that the project was intended to strengthen member associations but was cancelled because it created divisions that were no longer in the interest of the game.

He now intends to focus on restoring harmony and continuing to grow football globally, particularly in countries that need the most support.

headline: US F-35 fighter jet crashes near California military base
summary: The pilot safely ejected before impact; the aircraft, valued at approximately $109 million, was destroyed.
details: A US Marine Corps F-35B stealth fighter jet crashed on Friday near the Marine Corps Air Station Miramar in San Diego, California.
The pilot was able to eject from the aircraft before it hit the ground and was transported to a medical facility in stable condition.
The pilot is being treated for non-life-threatening injuries, according to military officials.
Footage from the scene showed a large plume of smoke rising from the wreckage as firefighters worked to extinguish the flames.
MCAS Miramar is globally recognized as the former home of the US Navy's elite 'Top Gun' school for pilots.
According to the manufacturer Lockheed Martin, each F-35B variant—capable of vertical takeoff and landing—costs approximately $109 million.
caption:
A $109 million US stealth fighter jet has crashed in California.

A US Marine Corps F-35B stealth fighter jet crashed on Friday near the Marine Corps Air Station Miramar in San Diego, California.

The pilot was able to eject from the aircraft before it hit the ground and was transported to a medical facility in stable condition.

The pilot is being treated for non-life-threatening injuries, according to military officials.

Footage from the scene showed a large plume of smoke rising from the wreckage as firefighters worked to extinguish the flames.

MCAS Miramar is globally recognized as the former home of the US Navy's elite 'Top Gun' school for pilots.

According to the manufacturer Lockheed Martin, each F-35B variant—capable of vertical takeoff and landing—costs approximately $109 million.
